corpus_definition: to move slowly without control, carried by water or wind

forms.definition: a slow movement of something carried by water or air
forms.example: The drift of the current took our ball far from the beach.

syn.note: General word; a drift is a slow movement you do not control.
The flow is the water or air itself moving; the drift is what it carries.

forms.definition: to move slowly without control, carried by water or wind
forms.example: The small boat began to drift out to sea.

syn.note: Easy word: to stay on water or in the air; drift adds the idea of slowly moving away.
Easy phrase with almost the same meaning: 'carried by the wind'.
Wander is for people or animals walking with no plan; drift is for things on water or in the air.

ant.note: To anchor a boat is to stop it moving, so it cannot drift.

forms.definition: floating on the water without control and not tied to anything
forms.example: After the engine stopped, the boat was adrift for two days.
forms.note: Used after a verb: 'be adrift', not before a noun.

syn.note: Floating means on the water; adrift adds that nobody controls it.
Lost is more general; adrift is for boats or things on water.

ant.note: An anchored boat is held in one place.

forms.note: No common -ly adverb. 'Adrift' is sometimes used like an adverb: 'The boat was cut adrift.' Drive shares a very old root with drift, but it is a different word, not made from drift.

people.definition: a person who moves from place to place with no fixed home or job
people.example: He lived like a drifter for years before he settled down.
people.note: Belongs to drift = live or move with no plan, not things carried by water or wind.

context.text: The fishing boat lost its engine and began to drift with the wind. By morning it was adrift far from the shore, and the coast guard had to find it.

reviewer_note: adrift kept as the adjective (a- is not in the affix table, so no affix claimed); drifter is other_meaning (aimless life).

corpus_definition: To fall in very small liquid drops.

forms.definition: a small drop of liquid that falls, or the sound it makes
forms.example: I could hear the drip of the kitchen tap all night.
forms.note: In hospitals, a drip is also a tube that puts liquid into your body.

syn.note: Easy word: one small round bit of liquid.
A trickle is a thin, slow line of liquid, a little more than drops.

forms.definition: to fall slowly as very small drops of liquid
forms.example: Water began to drip from the broken pipe.

syn.note: To flow slowly in a thin line; a little more liquid than drips.
To come out through a hole or crack by mistake; leaking water often drips.
To flow slowly in small amounts, often from a mouth or bottle.

ant.note: Liquid that pours comes out fast and in a large amount, not drop by drop.

forms.definition: very wet, with water falling off in drops
forms.example: He came in from the rain dripping wet.
forms.note: Often in the phrase 'dripping wet'.

syn.note: Completely wet.
Easy, general word; dripping is much wetter.

ant.note: With no water on it.

forms.definition: silly and too emotional, in a weak way
forms.example: It was a drippy love song with very boring words.
forms.note: Belongs to drip = a weak, boring person (informal), not falling drops of liquid.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: Our roof is old, and in spring water started to drip into the kitchen. My father went up to fix it in the rain and came down dripping wet.

reviewer_note: drippy listed as other_meaning (informal 'weak, silly'); medical drip mentioned only in a note.

corpus_definition: A long period with no rain at all.

forms.definition: a long time with little or no rain, when land becomes very dry
forms.example: The long drought killed all the farm crops.
forms.note: Pronounced /draʊt/, like 'out'.

syn.note: A period of dry weather; usually shorter and less serious than a drought.
Not enough water; often caused by a drought.

ant.note: Too much water covering the land, the opposite problem.

forms.note: No verb in this family.
Drought and dry come from the same old root, but dry is not made from drought. Say 'drought-hit' or 'dry'.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: Last summer there was a terrible drought in Karakalpakstan. The fields were dry for months, and many farmers lost their cotton.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; dry listed as not_family (shared root only).

corpus_definition: To die from being under water for too long.

forms.definition: a death caused by being under water for too long
forms.example: There are several drownings in the canals every summer.

syn.note: A plain way to explain it; drowning is the normal word.

forms.definition: to die because you are under water and cannot breathe
forms.example: The swimmer nearly drowned in the deep lake.
forms.note: Also used with an object: 'The flood drowned many animals.'

syn.note: Informal: to sink below the water, often before drowning.
To go down under water; a person who sinks may drown.

ant.note: To stay alive after something dangerous.

forms.definition: dead because of being under water for too long
forms.example: Rescuers found the drowned man near the bridge.

syn.note: General word; drowned says how the person died.

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

context.text: Never swim alone in the river, because people drown there every year. Last summer a lifeguard saved a young boy from drowning.

reviewer_note: Corpus example 'nearly did drown' is unnatural; map example uses 'nearly drowned'.

corpus_definition: The state of having no trouble or difficulty.

forms.definition: the state of having no trouble or difficulty
forms.example: She passed the exam with great ease.
forms.note: Most often in the phrase 'with ease'. 'At ease' means relaxed, a different meaning.

syn.note: The quality of not being difficult.
Doing something without needing much effort; less common.
Skill is the ability that often lets you do something with ease.

ant.note: 'With difficulty' is the opposite of 'with ease'.

forms.definition: to make a problem or process less difficult
forms.example: The new metro line will ease travel across the city.
forms.note: Also means to make pain or worry less: 'The medicine eased the pain.'

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same idea.
To make something less complicated.
To make pain or a problem less bad.

ant.note: To make something more difficult.

forms.definition: not difficult; needing little effort or skill
forms.example: The first part of the test was very easy.

syn.note: Very close; simple can also mean plain, not complicated.
Done without effort; a little formal.
Easy to understand or do, with no surprises.

ant.note: Needing a lot of effort or skill.
Everyday word for difficult.
Careful: uneasy means worried, the opposite of easy = relaxed, not of easy = simple.

forms.definition: without problems or much effort
forms.example: Bekzod easily found the way to the station.

syn.note: Without effort; a little formal.
Plain phrase with the same meaning.
With no problems, often about winning or having enough: 'won comfortably'.

ant.note: Needing a lot of effort.

context.text: Dilnoza speaks English with ease because she reads every day. The grammar test was easy for her, and she easily finished it in twenty minutes.

reviewer_note: easy/easily are from ease (Old French aise); uneasy put in ant with a note; easel is not family.

corpus_definition: The sound that is sent back to your ears.

forms.definition: a sound that comes back to you after hitting a wall or hill
forms.example: My shout made a loud echo in the cave.
forms.note: Plural: echoes.

syn.note: Formal or technical word for a sound that repeats.
General word for anything you hear.

forms.definition: to come back as a repeated sound after hitting a surface
forms.example: Our voices echoed in the empty school hall.
forms.note: Also means to repeat someone's words or ideas: 'She echoed her teacher's advice.'

syn.note: To be loud and fill a place with sound; a little formal.
Formal: to sound again and again.
'The hall rang with laughter': a place is full of sound.

forms.note: No common adjective. The participle 'echoing' is sometimes used before a noun: 'an echoing hall'.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: We visited a cave in the mountains near Samarkand, and my shout made a loud echo. Our voices echoed for a few seconds before it was quiet again.

reviewer_note: Noun and verb conversion only; echoing mentioned in note as participle, not a learner-dictionary adjective.

corpus_definition: all the living things in an area and how they interact together

forms.definition: all the plants and animals in one area and how they live together
forms.example: Pollution is destroying the ocean ecosystem at an alarming rate.

syn.note: The natural world around us; less about how living things depend on each other.
The natural home of one kind of animal or plant.
Easy, very general word for the natural world.

forms.note: No verb in this family.
Ecological comes from ecology, not from ecosystem. They share the part eco-.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: The Aral Sea ecosystem changed a lot when the water went away. Fish, birds and plants lost their homes, and the whole area became a desert.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; ecological/ecologist belong to ecology, listed as not_family.

corpus_definition: Doing something well without wasting time or energy.

forms.definition: the quality of working well without wasting time, money or energy
forms.example: The new machines improved the efficiency of the factory.

syn.note: How much work is done in a period of time.
Careful: effectiveness is about getting the result; efficiency is about not wasting anything.

ant.note: Wasting time, money or energy.
Using more than you need.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: working well and not wasting time or energy
forms.example: She is a very efficient worker.

syn.note: Planned and arranged well. British spelling: organised.
Producing a lot of work or results.
Careful: effective means it works; efficient means it works without waste.

ant.note: Wasting time, money or energy.
Using more than is needed.

forms.definition: in a quick and organized way, without wasting anything
forms.example: The new teacher runs the class very efficiently.

syn.note: In a way that produces a lot.
Easy, general word.

ant.note: In a way that wastes time or energy.

context.text: Our new washing machine is very efficient: it uses less water and electricity. Bekzod also works efficiently, so he often finishes his tasks early.

reviewer_note: effective vs efficient trap explained in syn notes; inefficient/inefficiency are antonyms, not forms.

corpus_definition: a process where people vote to choose who will lead the country

forms.definition: a time when people vote to choose a leader or government
forms.example: The national election happens every four years.

syn.note: An occasion when people choose by voting; can be about any decision, not only leaders.
Formal word for voting in an election; also a survey of opinions.
A secret vote, or the paper you vote on.

forms.definition: to choose someone for an important job by voting
forms.example: The people of the city elected a new mayor.

syn.note: One person votes for someone; many people together elect someone.
Easy, general word; elect means choosing by voting.
To choose carefully, not always by voting.

ant.note: To remove someone from a job by voting.

forms.definition: connected with choosing leaders by voting
forms.example: The country is planning electoral reform.

syn.note: Used before a noun: 'voting rights', 'the voting system'.
About government and power in general.

forms.definition: chosen by you, not something you must do
forms.example: In my last year at university I took an elective course in art.
forms.note: Belongs to elect = choose freely (optional courses, planned operations), not voting for leaders.
'Electorally' exists but is very rare and formal. Eligible (allowed to do something, e.g. vote) shares an old Latin root with elect, but it is not made from election.

people.definition: all the people in a country who have the right to vote
people.example: Young people are a big part of the electorate.

people.definition: a person who has the right to vote
people.example: Every elector must show a passport at the polling station.

context.text: Next year there will be an election in our city. People will elect a new mayor, and many young voters are excited to take part.

reviewer_note: election is made from elect; elective is other_meaning (optional); voter is the common word but not from this family.

corpus_definition: graceful and stylish in appearance or manner

forms.definition: the quality of looking or moving in a beautiful, stylish way
forms.example: Everyone admired the elegance of the old theatre in Tashkent.

syn.note: Beauty in the way someone moves or behaves.
A fashionable, attractive way of looking or doing things.
Easy, general word for being nice to look at.

ant.note: Moving in an awkward way that is not graceful.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: graceful and stylish in how someone looks or moves
forms.example: She looked elegant in her long blue dress.

syn.note: Fashionable and attractive.
Moving in a smooth, beautiful way.
British English: clean, neat and well dressed.
Easy, general word; elegant adds style and good taste.

ant.note: Untidy and dirty in how someone looks.
Moving in an awkward way.
Not stylish; a little formal.

forms.definition: in a graceful and stylish way
forms.example: The guests were elegantly dressed for the wedding.

syn.note: In a fashionable, attractive way.
In a smooth, beautiful way, often about moving.

ant.note: In an awkward way.

context.text: At her sister's wedding in Tashkent, Malika looked elegant in a long blue dress. She danced elegantly, and everyone talked about her elegance.

reviewer_note: -ance not in the affix table, so only -ly claimed; inelegant put in ant list.
